title: Pekudei: Moses blessed them (Exodus 39:43)
hook: Moses sees the finished work and blesses the workers

segments.voice: Yesterday, the refrain repeated through the last chapters: as the Lord commanded Moses. Your line was as it was asked. Which promise did you keep exactly? Day three hundred seventy-five.

The end of a big job has its own kind of quiet. A house renovated, a wedding pulled off, a school play performed, a garden finally planted. The people who did the work stand back, tired, a little proud, waiting. And very often, nobody says anything. The boss checks the list and moves on. The family is already planning the next thing. In the desert, the craftspeople bring every finished piece of the sanctuary to Moses: the tent, the ark, the curtains, the clothes. He looks it all over. And then he does the thing so many finished jobs never get.
screen: `THE END OF A BIG JOB.` → `OFTEN, NOBODY SAYS ANYTHING.` → `MOSES LOOKS IT ALL OVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the JPS 1917 translation: "And Moses saw all the work, and, behold, they had done it; as the LORD had commanded, even so had they done it. And Moses blessed them." Three steps. He sees. He recognizes that they did it right. And he blesses them. The rhythm has been heard before. At the end of the sixth day of creation, Genesis says: "And God saw every thing that He had made, and, behold, it was very good." Saw, and behold. Readers have noticed the echo, and more: the work is finished, the sanctuary is completed, a blessing is given, all language that recalls the creation of the world. Some readers hear the building of the sanctuary told as a small creation, with Moses looking at it the way God looked at the world. What did he say? The verse doesn't tell us. Rashi offers an answer from the midrash: Moses said, may it be God's will that the divine presence rest on the work of your hands. And Rashi connects it to Psalm ninety, which the Book of Psalms itself calls a prayer of Moses, and which ends by asking God to establish the work of our hands. So the first thing Moses does with the finished sanctuary isn't to use it, or to correct it, or to move on. It's to turn to the people who made it and bless them, and their hands.
screen: `HE SAW, AND BEHOLD.` · `AN ECHO OF CREATION.` · `MAY THE PRESENCE REST ON YOUR WORK.` · `ESTABLISH THE WORK OF OUR HANDS.` · then, large: `BLESS THE WORKERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see someone's finished work. Settle, and breathe. Think of something someone around you has finished recently: a report, a meal, a repair, a drawing, a hard semester, a hard year. Picture it clearly, the way Moses looked over every piece. Notice what they did well, specifically. Then think how you'll tell them: not a quick thanks, but a sentence that shows you really saw it, and that you wish good things for the work of their hands. The bell holds the time.
Pekudei. The portion where the work is finished, and Moses sees it, and blesses the people who made it.
Your line: bless the workers. Today, when someone finishes something, stop before you move on, and wish them well for the work of their hands. Day three hundred seventy-five.

screen: `DAY 375 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PEKUDEI: THE CLOUD FILLED IT.`

howItsDone: Psalm 90, which the Book of Psalms calls a prayer of Moses, is among the psalms added on Shabbat and festival mornings in the traditional prayer book; Rashi ties its last verse, establish the work of our hands, to Moses' blessing here.

options: check it all, then bless the people who made it.

original.note: Hebrew: and Moses blessed them, the end of Exodus 39:43.

trapdoor: what you thought: Moses said a few kind words.
what it means: Moses sees the finished work, recognizes it was done right, and blesses the workers.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on 39:43 gives the blessing as 'may the Shechinah rest on the work of your hands' and links it to Psalm 90:17; the verse echoes Genesis 1:31 and 2:1–3.
